title: The Lumières made a knocked-down wall leap back up by projecting their film backwards

cover.alt: Black-and-white 1890s film still: a tall slab of wall topples beside a house as a man in a waistcoat watches and two workers lean on poles.

body: In *Démolition d’un mur*, an 1890s Lumière film, workers push over a wall in a cloud of dust. The Lumière brothers sometimes projected it in reverse, so the dust gathered up and the wall sprang back into place. Showing action backwards has been a film-maker’s tool ever since, for magic and for practical reasons. It is almost impossible for a helicopter to swoop down and end on a perfectly framed, focused close-up, so such shots are filmed starting close to the target and pulling away, then run in reverse.

slides.alt: Black-and-white 1890s film: workers push over a tall wall, which falls in a huge cloud of dust; then the same shot runs backwards, the dust rushes in and the wall stands up again.
slides.caption: Démolition d’un mur, shown here forwards and then in reverse, as the Lumières sometimes projected it: the dust gathers up and the wall springs back.
slides.credit: Louis Lumière · Public domain · excerpt, shown forwards then reversed

slides.prompt: In Coldplay’s video for The Scientist, time runs backwards but Chris Martin seems to sing normally. How did he manage it?
slides.answer: A month learning the lyrics backwards
slides.detail: Someone moving against reversed time may need to perform every action backwards during filming, singing included. Martin trained for a whole month.

slides.heading: Cocteau’s recurring trick
slides.text: Jean Cocteau used reverse action all through his films. In Beauty and the Beast (1946) an actor put a piece of paper in a fire and walked backwards away; reversed, he seems to walk up and pull it out. By Le Testament d’Orphée, more than one critic called the trick an embarrassing personal tic.

slides.question: Why might a car that must stop just short of an actor be filmed in reverse?
slides.explanation: The car starts at the stopping point and drives away; reversed, it seems to brake just in time. Tomorrow Never Dies used it for a car stopping centimetres from Bond and Q.
